communityImage.caption: St. Basil's Cathedral, Moscow, in an etching from about 1900. Russian speakers in Minnesota also have roots in Ukraine, Belarus, Moldova, Central Asia, the Caucasus and elsewhere.

people.name: Leonid Hurwicz
body: On December 10, 2007, a 90-year-old professor emeritus sat on the stage of Ted Mann Concert Hall at the University of Minnesota while the Nobel ceremony in Stockholm played by satellite. Too frail to travel, Leonid Hurwicz received the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences from the Swedish ambassador. The academy said at the time that he was the oldest Nobel winner ever. Older laureates have followed since.

He was born in Moscow on August 21, 1917, to Polish parents, and in early 1919 the family returned to Warsaw. There he stood at the back of a university classroom for a year with other Jewish students, refusing a segregated section. He finished a law degree in 1938, went to the London School of Economics, and was in Switzerland when Germany invaded Poland. His parents and brother escaped east and were sent to a Soviet labor camp in the Arctic. He crossed Spain to Portugal, tutored children in Estoril for almost two months, and reached the United States in 1940 by Greek boat.

The only degree his Nobel biography names is the one in law. He learned economics by auditing courses in Chicago and working as an assistant to Paul Samuelson at MIT. During the war he taught statistics and mathematics at the University of Chicago's Institute of Meteorology. In 1951, while at the University of Illinois, he resigned in protest when politically liberal colleagues were targeted during the McCarthy years. A friend suggested Minnesota, and within months he had moved his family to Minneapolis, where he stayed for the rest of his life and became a Regents Professor.

His prize, shared with Eric Maskin and Roger Myerson, was for the foundations of mechanism design theory, which asks how to write rules so that people acting in their own interest still produce good results. It helps economists judge trading mechanisms, regulation and voting procedures. He died in Minneapolis on June 24, 2008.
keyFacts: 1940: Reaches the United States as a refugee.
1951: Moves to the University of Minnesota.
2007: Shares the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences; receives it in Minneapolis on December 10.
people.connectToWork: When a rule you apply asks people to report something about themselves, what does the rule reward them for saying, and what could it cost them to be accurate?

people.name: Pitirim Sorokin
body: In 1922 a sociology professor who had once been condemned to death by the Bolsheviks left Soviet Russia for good. Friends including the Czech leaders Tomáš Masaryk and Edvard Beneš helped him find asylum. Two years later Pitirim Sorokin was teaching at the University of Minnesota.

Sorokin was born on January 21, 1889, in the village of Turya in the far north of the Russian Empire. The American Sociological Association describes him as a Komi peasant, and his mother died when he was three. He became the first professor of sociology at the University of St. Petersburg and served as secretary to Alexander Kerensky, which put his life in danger after 1917. He was captured, condemned to death and held in prison before friends intervened, and the Soviet government finally forced him out.

After lecturing at Wisconsin and Illinois he moved to Minnesota in 1924. His books from those years include The Sociology of Revolution (1925), Social Mobility (1927), Contemporary Sociological Theories (1928) and, with Carle C. Zimmerman, Principles of Rural-Urban Sociology (1929). Social mobility, the study of how people move up or down in society, became a core idea of the field.

In 1930 Harvard hired him to found its sociology department. After a 1963 write-in campaign, the first successful write-in nomination in the association's history, he became the 55th president of the American Sociological Association and gave his presidential address in 1965. He died in Winchester, Massachusetts, on February 10, 1968.
keyFacts: 1889: Born January 21 in Turya, northern Russia.
1924: Begins teaching at the University of Minnesota.
1965: Gives his presidential address to the American Sociological Association.
people.connectToWork: When a form asks for one nationality or one language, whose background does that answer hide, and what could you ask instead?

people.name: Mikhail Shifman
body: In March 2017, at the International Centre for Theoretical Physics, two University of Minnesota physicists stood together to receive one of their field's highest honors, the Dirac Medal. One was Mikhail Shifman, who had come to Minnesota from Moscow decades earlier.

Born in Riga, Latvia, in 1949, Shifman graduated from the Moscow Institute of Physics and Technology in 1972 and earned his Ph.D. in 1976 at Moscow's Institute for Theoretical and Experimental Physics. With Arkady Vainshtein and Valentine Zakharov he developed what physicists call the SVZ sum rules, which relate the observed properties of hadrons, the particles bound by the strong force, to properties of the vacuum.

He joined the University of Minnesota's William I. Fine Theoretical Physics Institute in 1990. As of October 2026 the university lists him as a professor holding the Ida Cohen Fine Chair in Theoretical Physics. His honors include the Sakurai Prize (1999), the Pomeranchuk Prize (2013) and the 2016 Dirac Medal, shared with Vainshtein and Nathan Seiberg. He was elected to the National Academy of Sciences in 2018.
keyFacts: 1976: Ph.D., Institute for Theoretical and Experimental Physics, Moscow.
1990: Joins the University of Minnesota faculty.
2016: Dirac Medal, with Vainshtein and Seiberg.
2018: Elected to the National Academy of Sciences.

people.name: Arkady Vainshtein
body: Siberia's science city of Novosibirsk trained some of the Soviet Union's leading physicists. One of them, Arkady Vainshtein, went on to spend more than three decades in Minneapolis and helped lead the University of Minnesota's theoretical physics institute.

Vainshtein earned an M.S. from Novosibirsk University in 1964 and a Ph.D. from the Budker Institute of Nuclear Physics in 1968. His collaboration with Mikhail Shifman and Valentine Zakharov, begun in Moscow more than forty years before the 2016 Dirac Medal, produced the SVZ sum rules for understanding the strong nuclear force.

Born in 1942, he became a professor at the University of Minnesota in 1990 and a U.S. citizen in 1998. He directed the William I. Fine Theoretical Physics Institute from 1993 to 1996 and held the Gloria Becker Lubkin chair from 1990 to 2018. As of October 2026 the university lists him as professor emeritus. His honors include the Sakurai Prize (1999), the Pomeranchuk Prize (2005), the Julius Wess Award (2014) and the 2016 Dirac Medal.
keyFacts: 1968: Ph.D., Budker Institute of Nuclear Physics, Novosibirsk.
1990: Becomes a professor at the University of Minnesota.
2016: Dirac Medal, with Shifman and Seiberg.
people.connectToWork: When someone arrives with decades of professional standing elsewhere, what does your first conversation assume about what they know and what they need?

people.name: Kirill Kaprizov
body: On January 14, 2021, in his first NHL game, Kirill Kaprizov scored the overtime winner for the Minnesota Wild against the Los Angeles Kings. The NHL Players' Association counted him as only the third player to do that in a debut. Wild fans had waited more than five years for him to arrive.

Kaprizov was born on April 26, 1997, in the Siberian industrial city of Novokuznetsk. The Wild drafted him in the fifth round in 2015, 135th overall, and he spent five more seasons in Russia's Kontinental Hockey League, winning the Gagarin Cup with CSKA Moscow in 2019, before signing with Minnesota in July 2020. At the 2018 Olympics he won gold with the Olympic Athletes from Russia, scoring the power-play overtime winner in the 4-3 final against Germany and leading the tournament with five goals.

He won the Calder Trophy as NHL rookie of the year for 2020–21, the first Wild player to do so. In September 2025 he signed an eight-year, $136 million extension through 2033-34, at the time the richest contract in NHL history by average annual value.
keyFacts: 2015: Drafted 135th overall by the Minnesota Wild.
2021: NHL debut January 14; wins the Calder Trophy for 2020–21.
people.connectToWork: A public figure may be the only Russian speaker some of your colleagues can name. What do you know about the Russian speakers your own work reaches, and how did you learn it?

people.name: Vladimir Zworykin
body: In 1929 a Russian-born engineer demonstrated an all-electronic television system to a convention of radio engineers and perfected a picture tube he called the kinescope. With his camera tube, the iconoscope, Vladimir Zworykin helped make electronic television real.

Zworykin was born in Murom, east of Moscow. Britannica gives 1888 and the National Academy of Sciences memoir gives 1889. He served in the Russian Signal Corps in World War I, fled after the revolution and settled in the United States in 1919. At Westinghouse in Pittsburgh, executives were unimpressed by his early television demonstrations. David Sarnoff of RCA backed him, and by 1930 he was at RCA's laboratory in Camden, New Jersey, heading its television research. He also contributed to the electron microscope. He received the National Medal of Science in 1966 and died in Princeton on July 29, 1982.
keyFacts: 1930: Heads television research at RCA in Camden, New Jersey.
1982: Dies July 29 in Princeton, New Jersey.
people.connectToWork: Zworykin's first employer did not see what his work could do, and another did. Who in your organization decides whether a newcomer's skills count, and on what evidence?

people.name: Sergey Brin
body: On October 25, 1979, a six-year-old boy landed at New York's Kennedy Airport with his family, who had left Moscow mainly because of antisemitism. His father, a mathematician, had been fired after the family applied to emigrate. That boy, Sergey Brin, would co-found Google.

Born August 21, 1973, Brin came through Vienna, where the Hebrew Immigrant Aid Society met the family, and spent months near Paris before reaching America. He earned a degree in computer science and mathematics at the University of Maryland in 1993 and went on to Stanford, where he and Larry Page built the search engine. He stepped down as president of Alphabet in 2019. In 2009, on the 30th anniversary of his family's arrival, he gave $1 million to HIAS, and his family has given heavily to Parkinson's disease research.
keyFacts: 1979: Family arrives in the United States on October 25.
1993: Degree from the University of Maryland.
people.connectToWork: Brin's father lost his job for asking to leave. What would a person with that kind of history want to know about where their information goes before they fill out your form?

people.name: Mikhail Baryshnikov
body: On June 29, 1974, while on tour in Toronto, a star of Leningrad's Kirov Ballet slipped away after a performance and asked Canada for asylum. Mikhail Baryshnikov's defection became one of the Cold War's best-known cultural stories.

Born in Riga on January 27, 1948, to Russian parents, he trained at the Vaganova school and made his Kirov debut in 1967. In the West he danced with American Ballet Theatre and led it as artistic director for about a decade from 1980. He became a U.S. citizen on July 3, 1986, and became a Latvian citizen in 2017. He earned an Academy Award nomination for best supporting actor for The Turning Point (1977), received Kennedy Center Honors in 2000 and opened the Baryshnikov Arts Center in New York in 2004.
keyFacts: 1980: Becomes artistic director of American Ballet Theatre.
people.connectToWork: A person can be born in Latvia to Russian parents, leave through Canada and hold U.S. and Latvian citizenship. Which of your fields would flatten that, and does the difference matter for the decision you make?

people.name: Ayn Rand
body: On February 18, 1926, a young woman from Leningrad arrived in New York City with fifty dollars. She never returned to the Soviet Union. She would become Ayn Rand, one of the best-selling American novelists of the 20th century.

Rand was born Alisa Zinovievna Rosenbaum on February 2, 1905, in Saint Petersburg, the eldest daughter of a Jewish merchant. She lived through the revolution as a girl and graduated with highest honors in 1924 from the University of Leningrad. After about six months with relatives in Chicago, she moved to Hollywood to pursue screenwriting. She became a U.S. citizen on March 13, 1931.

A dozen publishers turned down The Fountainhead before it appeared in 1943; it went on to sell millions of copies. Atlas Shrugged followed in 1957. Through her novels and essays she developed a philosophy she called Objectivism. She died in New York City on March 6, 1982.
keyFacts: 1982: Dies March 6 in New York City.
people.connectToWork: Rand's views of government grew from what she saw of one. How might someone's experience of a past government shape how they hear an offer of help from yours, and how would you find out rather than guess?

people.name: Emma Goldman
body: On December 21, 1919, aboard the transport ship Buford, nicknamed the Red Ark, Emma Goldman and 248 other foreign-born radicals were deported from the United States to Soviet Russia. She had spent three decades as one of America's best-known and most controversial speakers.

Goldman was born on June 27, 1869, in the Jewish quarter of Kovno, then in the Russian Empire and now Kaunas, Lithuania. Antisemitism pushed her family to Königsberg and then to Saint Petersburg. She left for the United States in 1885 and worked in the garment industry in Rochester, New York. In 1889 she moved to New York's Lower East Side.

She became a leading anarchist lecturer and writer and published the magazine Mother Earth from 1906 to 1917. Her anti-conscription organizing during World War I led to eighteen months in federal prison. On her release she was re-arrested on the order of J. Edgar Hoover, and that December she and Alexander Berkman were deported. Disillusioned by Bolshevik repression, she left Soviet Russia in December 1921 and published My Disillusionment in Russia in 1923. She later wrote the autobiography Living My Life. She died in Toronto on May 14, 1940, and was buried in Chicago's Waldheim Cemetery.
keyFacts: 1869: Born June 27 in Kovno, Russian Empire.
1885: Leaves for the United States and settles in Rochester.
1919: Deported to Soviet Russia on December 21.
people.connectToWork: Goldman's immigration status became tied to what she said in public. If someone you serve fears that speaking up could affect their status, what can you truthfully tell them, and who confirms it?

people.name: Regina Spektor
body: In 1989, during perestroika, nine-year-old Regina Spektor and her musical family left Moscow. They had to leave behind the family piano, a gift from her grandfather to her mother. They spent months in transit through Austria and Italy and entered the United States as refugees with help from HIAS. The family settled in the Bronx.

By her account, the family could not attend synagogue in the Soviet Union and faced discrimination as Jews. In the Bronx her father worked nights developing photos for minimum wage, and with no piano at home she practiced in the basement of a neighborhood synagogue. She attended SAR Academy, a Jewish day school in Riverdale, and later high schools in New Jersey, studied piano at the Manhattan School of Music until 17 and graduated with honors from the Purchase College Conservatory of Music in 2001.

She built a following in New York's downtown music scene, signed with Sire Records in 2004 and reached a national audience with Begin to Hope (2006). Later albums include Far (2009), What We Saw from the Cheap Seats (2012), Remember Us to Life (2016) and Home, before and after (2022). You've Got Time, her theme for Orange Is the New Black, earned a Grammy nomination at the 2014 awards. New York City declared June 11, 2019, Regina Spektor Day. She performed at a 2012 New York benefit for HIAS.
keyFacts: 1989: Family arrives as refugees with help from HIAS.
2001: Graduates from Purchase College Conservatory of Music.
2014: Grammy nomination for You've Got Time.
2019: Regina Spektor Day in New York City.
people.connectToWork: What training or talent might a new arrival be working to keep alive, and does anything in your process ask about it or get in its way?

people.name: Nastia Liukin
body: In August 2008 in Beijing, an 18-year-old from Texas won the Olympic all-around gold medal in women's gymnastics. Nastia Liukin had been born in Moscow and grew up in a gym her Soviet-champion father co-founded in America.

Liukin was born on October 30, 1989. Her father, Valeri Liukin, won two gold medals for the Soviet Union at the 1988 Olympics, and her mother, Anna Kotchneva, was a 1987 world clubs champion in rhythmic gymnastics. After the Soviet Union dissolved in 1991, the family emigrated when she was two and a half and settled in Plano, Texas, where her father co-founded the World Olympic Gymnastics Academy and coached her.

She won world titles on balance beam in 2005 and 2007 and on uneven bars in 2005, and team gold with the U.S. in 2007. In Beijing she won five medals: gold in the all-around, silver on beam, bars and in the team event, and bronze on floor. She entered the International Gymnastics Hall of Fame in 2018 and the U.S. Olympic and Paralympic Hall of Fame with the Class of 2019.
keyFacts: After 1991: Family moves to Plano, Texas.
2008: Olympic all-around gold and five medals in Beijing.
2019: U.S. Olympic and Paralympic Hall of Fame.
people.connectToWork: When a family rebuilds a profession in a new country, which of your programs would treat that as a strength, and which would only see an income change?

people.name: Julia Ioffe
body: In 1990 a seven-year-old girl and her family left Moscow, a month before she was to finish first grade, and came to the United States. Two decades later, Julia Ioffe was back in Moscow as a correspondent, explaining Russia to American readers.

Ioffe grew up in Columbia, Maryland, attended Beth Tfiloh Dahan Community School in Baltimore and graduated from Princeton in 2005 with a history major and a certificate in Russian studies. With a Fulbright scholarship she returned to Moscow in 2009 and spent three years reporting for The New Yorker and Foreign Policy. Her 2011 profile of Alexei and Yulia Navalny was recognized by the Livingston Awards for journalists under 35.

Her work has appeared in The New Republic, Politico, The Atlantic, The New York Times Magazine and The Washington Post, among others. In 2021 she became a founding partner of the media company Puck, where as of October 2026 she is Washington correspondent. In 2025 she published Motherland: A Feminist History of Modern Russia, from Revolution to Autocracy, which traces Russian history through women's lives, including those of her own family. It was a National Book Award finalist and won a National Jewish Book Award.
keyFacts: 1990: Family arrives in the United States.
2021: Becomes a founding partner of Puck.
people.connectToWork: Who in a family carried the paperwork and the appointments through a move between countries, and does your process quietly depend on that same person now?

people.name: Masha Gessen
body: In July 2024 a Moscow court sentenced Masha Gessen to eight years in prison, in absentia, for comments about Russia's war in Ukraine. Gessen was in New York, where they had lived since leaving Russia in 2013, and had become one of America's best-known writers on authoritarianism. They use they/them pronouns and write as M. Gessen.

Gessen was born in Moscow in 1967 and came to the United States with their family in 1981 as a teenager, during an earlier wave of Soviet-Jewish emigration. In the early 1990s they moved back to Moscow and worked there as a journalist and editor for more than twenty years.

Their books include The Man Without a Face (2012), Words Will Break Cement (2014), The Brothers (2015) and Surviving Autocracy (2020). The Future Is History (2017) won the National Book Award for Nonfiction. Gessen was a staff writer at The New Yorker from 2017 to 2024 and joined The New York Times as an opinion columnist that year. As of October 2026 they remain a Times columnist, and they won the 2026 Pulitzer Prize for Opinion Writing.
keyFacts: 1981: Family emigrates to the United States.
1990s: Returns to Moscow as a journalist.
2017: National Book Award for The Future Is History.
2024: Sentenced in absentia by a Moscow court; joins The New York Times.
2026: Pulitzer Prize for Opinion Writing, for work in The New York Times.
people.connectToWork: Some Russian speakers settled decades ago and some left recently because of war or threat. Does your process treat them as one group, and what would change if you asked when and why a person came?

people.name: Vladimir Nabokov
body: On May 19, 1940, a Russian writer, his wife Véra and their young son Dmitri sailed from Saint-Nazaire, France, on the Champlain, bound for New York, weeks before Paris fell. Vladimir Nabokov was already the leading novelist of the Russian emigration. In America he would reinvent himself as an English-language writer.

Nabokov was born in Saint Petersburg on April 22, 1899. His family went into exile in 1919, first to England. From 1922 he lived in Berlin, writing in Russian, and he left in 1937, after Véra, who was half Jewish, lost her job in 1936 under the Nazis. The family spent the next few years in France.

In the United States he taught at Wellesley College and then, from 1948 until the late 1950s, at Cornell University. Through the 1940s he also studied butterflies at Harvard's Museum of Comparative Zoology. He became a U.S. citizen in 1945. Lolita, published in 1955, was later translated by Nabokov himself into Russian, and Pale Fire followed in 1962. He died in Montreux, Switzerland, on July 2, 1977.
people.connectToWork: Nabokov changed the language he wrote in at about 40. When you judge how well someone manages in English, what might you be missing about what they can do in another language?

people.name: Ivanova Smith
body: Ivanova Smith spent her first five years in an institutional orphanage in Soviet-controlled Latvia. She has said she remembers no friends or toys, and that she would stare at a light for entertainment. She was born with intellectual and developmental disabilities, and when she was adopted at 5 she still did not speak.

She learned English, got through bullying and self-doubt and graduated from high school. At Central Washington University, a history major and in her words an IDD student, she wrote her thesis on the history of eugenics, a movement that would once have labeled her defective. When she became pregnant she feared her daughter would be taken from her.

In a first-person article published by the University of Minnesota's Institute on Community Integration, she describes being taught self-hatred in special education before she learned about the disability civil rights movement. The American Civil Liberties Union of Washington lists her as Chair of Self Advocates in Leadership and as Advocate Faculty at the University of Washington's LEND program. Her published accounts do not say whether she speaks Russian or belongs to a Russian-speaking community, and she lives in Washington, not Minnesota. She appears here because her life links Soviet-era institutions to American self-advocacy.

Wrote a university thesis on the history of eugenics.

people.connectToWork: If a family's only experience of disability services was an institution, what would they need to see or hear from you before believing another option is real, and how would you hear from the disabled person directly?

people.name: Alfiya Battalova
body: At 16, Alfiya Battalova left Omsk, Russia, for a year as an exchange student at a Minnesota high school. In her words it felt like a revelation that people with disabilities can be treated with dignity, with ramps, elevators and a general sense of accessibility. She adds that she had not yet realized how much remained to be done in the United States too.

Back in Russia she studied regional studies at Omsk State University and, with other exchange alumni, gave presentations on the problems disabled people faced. A Fulbright scholarship took her to the University of Maine for a master's in public administration, chosen for its disability studies program, and she interned at the Center for Disability Rights in New York. She wrote that she wanted to push forward a disability rights agenda in Russia and that its old medical and benefits-based approach leaves no room for the full potential of Russian society.

She went on to earn a doctorate. As of October 2026 her own website describes her as an academic researcher and program evaluation specialist in disability studies, health professions education and community-based research. Her comparison is one person's view, written early in her career, and does not describe what any family expects.
keyFacts: Exchange year at a Minnesota high school at 16.
Fulbright scholar; master's program at the University of Maine.
Interned at the Center for Disability Rights.
Now a researcher and evaluator in disability studies.

institutions.name: The Museum of Russian Art
body: In south Minneapolis, a Spanish Colonial-Revival building that was once the Mayflower Congregational Church, and later a funeral home, holds a museum devoted to Russian art and culture. The Museum of Russian Art, known as TMORA, was founded by Minnesota collectors Raymond and Susan Johnson.

It became a nonprofit in 2002 and opened its first exhibition that year in Bloomington. The founders' 2002 gift of seven paintings started the permanent collection. The museum bought the former church in early 2004, remodeled it in a way that keeps its original character, and moved there in 2005.

The museum says it holds more than thirteen thousand works: paintings, sculpture, Soviet-era posters, art made outside official Soviet rules, folk art, nesting dolls, lacquer boxes and samovars, with 95 percent from Russia within its 1991 borders. It states a commitment to an independent voice, free of influence from foreign governments or political actors. As of October 2026 its galleries include Say No to War, political cartoons by Ukrainian and Russian artists.
keyFacts: 2002: Becomes a nonprofit; first exhibition in Bloomington.
2005: Moves to the former Mayflower church in south Minneapolis.
Holds more than thirteen thousand works, by its own count.
institutions.connectToWork: If your team wanted to learn about Russian-speaking Minnesotans at a place like this, what would you still need to hear from people themselves, including those with no tie to Russia?

institutions.name: St. Mary's Orthodox Cathedral
institutions.type: Place of worship, Orthodox Church in America
body: In 1891 a small immigrant congregation in northeast Minneapolis was received into the Orthodox Church. That decision made St. Mary's one of the founding parishes of Russian Orthodoxy among immigrants in America, and its founders were not Russians.

The parish began in 1887 as an Eastern-rite Catholic community of Carpatho-Rusyn immigrants, most from villages north of Prešov in present-day eastern Slovakia, then in the Austro-Hungarian Empire. Their first resident priest, Father Alexis Toth, recorded his arrival on November 28, 1889, and led them into Orthodoxy under the Russian church. He was canonized in 1994.

The first church burned in 1904. The present building went up in 1905, the same year the first Russian Orthodox seminary in America was established here through the efforts of St. Tikhon, who consecrated the cathedral in 1906. Today it is a cathedral of the Orthodox Church in America's Diocese of the Midwest.
institutions.connectToWork: If a person says "Russian Orthodox", what have you learned about their language, ancestry or nationality? What would you ask rather than assume?

institutions.name: Jewish Family and Children's Service of Minnesota
aliases: Jewish Family and Children's Service of Minneapolis
body: In February 1910, community members in Minneapolis met to plan help for Jewish refugees expected from Europe. That meeting started the agency now called Jewish Family and Children's Service, first known as the Associated Jewish Charities of Minneapolis.

In its first year it served 345 families with food, shelter, a dispensary, loans, an employment bureau and a home for travelers. It helped Eastern European Jewish immigrants find work and medical care, and in 1947 it placed Holocaust survivor Reva Kibort in foster care.

By its chief executive's 2017 account, JFCS and Jewish Family Service of St. Paul resettled well over 1,000 families from the former Soviet Union from the late 1980s through the 1990s. That count comes from the agency. MNopedia confirms that Soviet Jewish resettlement programs ran in those years but gives no number. As of October 2026 the agency runs senior and caregiver services, including Holocaust survivor support, mental health counseling, waiver case management, vocational rehabilitation and MFIP career services, and a Jewish Community Inclusion Program for People with Disabilities. Its home page lists no Russian-language program, so ask.
keyFacts: 1910: Founded in Minneapolis as the Associated Jewish Charities.
1910: Serves 345 families in its first year.
Late 1980s–1990s: With Jewish Family Service of St. Paul, resettles well over 1,000 families from the former Soviet Union, by its own count.

institutions.name: Disability Hub MN
body: Disability Hub MN is a free statewide resource that helps people with disabilities solve problems and plan for the future across health, money, housing, work and family supports. It launched in 2006. Its tools include Disability Benefits 101 and Housing Benefits 101.

Its website says "We serve all languages", and people can call, chat or email. We did not find written Russian content on the home page, so ask for an interpreter and ask what is available in writing. The Hub also appears in the statewide routes on this page.
institutions.connectToWork: When you refer someone to a statewide line, have you checked what happens when a Russian speaker actually calls it?

disability.intro: This is background for preparing questions. It does not describe any person or family. Here, Russian-speaking means people who use Russian, whatever their nationality, faith or generation: Jewish, Russian Orthodox, Ukrainian, Belarusian, Baltic, Central Asian and Caucasian families among them, some here since Soviet times and some arriving after 2022. We did not find a peer-reviewed study of disability among Russian-speaking immigrants in Minnesota. Most of what follows comes from research in Russia, which is a related setting and not the same one.
questions: Which language do you want to use with us: Russian, Ukrainian, Yiddish, English or another? Is this interpreter a good fit for you?
What were you told about this condition, here or back home?
How do you and your family understand what's going on? What words do you use for it, in any language?
Has anyone given you a diagnosis or a label? Has it helped?
What would you want a disability label or assessment to open up for you? Is there anything you want it to avoid?
Who do you want involved in decisions, and is there anyone you don't want involved?
Have past experiences with doctors, schools, institutions or government offices, here or elsewhere, affected how you feel about getting services? What would make this feel safer?
What do you want to know about where your information goes before you share it?
Is faith or a congregation important to you, and would it help to connect services with it?
Are you connected to other families or groups who speak your language? Would you like to be?

context.heading: What research in Russia describes
body: A study in Tatarstan interviewed parents of children with Down syndrome, Rett syndrome or autism, along with professionals, in 2013–2014 and 2018–2019. It reports stigma in both special and mainstream preschools, and parents moving "from secrecy and withdrawal to resistance". In Kazan some parents set up groups for autistic children inside mainstream kindergartens. The authors call for clear information for parents, more trained specialists and work against stigma (Kuznetsova, Garapshina and Mukharyamova, 2021). The abstract gives no sample size.

A 2006 Macalester College honors thesis, an ethnography of one impoverished Siberian village, found that "the stigma of disability is branded on the mother of an impaired child". The same mothers organized their own grassroots school (Hartblay, 2006). This is one village, twenty years ago.

If someone has lived through systems like these, they may have reasons to be careful about disclosing a disability. That is an inference from research in Russia, not a finding about Minnesota families, and it tells you nothing about the person you are meeting.

sources.label: Kuznetsova, Garapshina and Mukharyamova, Journal of Children's Services 16(4), 2021, abstract
Hartblay, An Absolutely Different Life, Macalester College, 2006

context.heading: What U.S. and Minnesota sources add
body: A 2019 Rutgers dissertation interviewed 20 Russian-speaking immigrants aged 36 to 83 on the East Coast. It found that how people saw health and illness was tied to how they saw health care, and that ties across borders shaped beliefs and practices among those who came after the Soviet Union dissolved. It cites earlier work reporting low use of preventive care and screening. It is small, it is not about disability, and its author calls for study of other groups and places (Amburg, 2019).

Culture Care Connection, a Minnesota health equity resource, says data on Russian Americans is limited and may not apply in Minnesota. It reports from 2013 research that immigrants aged 50 to 84 from the former Soviet Union described more limits in daily activities than U.S.-born white people, and fewer than their peers in Russia. That page gives no sample size.

In a 2016 MinnPost article, Gedaly Meerovich, who founded the Slavic Community Center, said parents he knew were often reluctant to seek help for a child's drug use because of shame. That is one community leader's view, about drug use and not disability. Other sources do not document who makes decisions in Russian-speaking households in the U.S., or spiritual explanations of disability. Do not assume either; ask.

sources.label: Amburg, Traditional health-related practices of Russian-speaking immigrants residing in the United States, Rutgers University, 2019
Culture Care Connection, Russian
MinnPost, How the Russian-speaking community became Minnesota's invisible immigrants (June 2016)

context.heading: Words, systems and what to explain
body: Alfiya Battalova, profiled on this page, wrote from her own experience in Omsk about Russia's "medical and benefits-based approach to disability". Someone raised with that system may or may not expect it here. Say plainly what U.S. disability services offer, including rights, choice and community living, and let the person tell you what they expected.

Ivanova Smith, also profiled here, calls herself an IDD student in one interview and writes about the word defective from the history of eugenics. Follow each person's own language. We did not find a reliable source on which Russian disability terms people prefer today, so ask, and check with the interpreter how a term lands.

Explain what information goes where, and what affects immigration status only after checking with a legal or immigration resource rather than from memory. Written translations help, and it also helps to have a person go through them with the family. We did not find a Minnesota disability organization specific to Russian speakers; the search was limited, so do not treat any one group as speaking for everyone.

communityRoutes.name: Jewish Family and Children's Service of Minnesota
communityRoutes.purpose: Runs a Jewish Community Inclusion Program for People with Disabilities, waiver case management, vocational rehabilitation and mental health counseling. Open to the Jewish and general community. Ask about Russian-language help when you call, 952-546-0616.

communityRoutes.name: Nasha Shkola Charter School
communityRoutes.purpose: A public K–8 charter school in Brooklyn Park focused on Russian language and culture. As a public school it has special education duties, so families there can raise concerns or requests with the school. 763-496-5550.

organizations.intro: Counts of Russian speakers in Minnesota vary because they measure different things. Community leaders put it at about 60,000, and the State Demographic Center's estimate of people claiming Russian ancestry was 43,000 in a 2016 MinnPost article and 48,000 in an undated Culture Care Connection page. Macalester College, undated, gives a Russian population of more than 12,500 and, separately, more than 2,300 public school students who speak Russian at home. In 2023 a local publisher put immigrants from the region in the Twin Cities at 56,000. None of these is a full count of Russian speakers: the 60,000 is an estimate from community leaders, and the others measure ancestry, origin or one age group. There is no single neighborhood: people live across the metro, including St. Louis Park, Plymouth, Eden Prairie and Savage. By MinnPost's 2016 account they have built churches, charter and private schools, newspapers, businesses and a museum. This list is a starting point for learning, is not complete, and says nothing about who a person trusts. Some groups named here have religious or political positions of their own.

entries.name: Russian-American Jews in Minnesota
entries.type: Cultural and faith, young families and teens
entries.purpose: Says it has served the Russian-speaking Jewish community since 2003. Runs a Teen Fellowship (registration open for 2026–27), educational and cultural programs, conferences and volunteer missions.

entries.name: Minneapolis Jewish Federation
entries.purpose: Macalester College's undated page says it sponsors programs for the Russian émigré community in the Twin Cities. The Federation's own home page does not mention them, so ask what runs today.

entries.name: Minnesota JCC
entries.purpose: Formed in 2021 from the St. Paul JCC and Sabes JCC. A state aging-resources listing updated in February 2026 says some monthly senior outings are held in Russian. Its own site does not describe Russian-language programs, so ask.

entries.name: St. Panteleimon Russian Orthodox Church
entries.type: Faith, Russian Orthodox Church Outside Russia
entries.purpose: A parish that marked its 70th anniversary in August 2026. Posts its schedule in Russian and English, and has a sisterhood and a Sunday school. 612-517-7496.

entries.name: Russian Orthodox Church and Skete of the Resurrection of Christ
entries.purpose: Says services are in Church Slavonic and English, with sermons in Russian and English.

entries.name: Holy Trinity Orthodox Church
entries.purpose: Founded in 1916 by Belorussian and Serbian working-class communities and known until 1990 as the Russian-Serbian Orthodox Church. The church's directory listing says services are now in English and describes a mixed congregation of Palestinian, Greek, Serbian, Russian and other backgrounds.

entries.name: St. Herman's Orthodox Church
entries.purpose: Founded in 1976. East-West Connections lists it among Russian-language churches in Minnesota, while St. Herman's own site says it serves in English and that most parishioners are converts. Ask about language before referring anyone.

entries.name: Russian Educational Center of Minnesota
entries.purpose: Founded in 2002 by parent volunteers. Offers Russian classes for children from age 3½, Russian as a foreign language and a course for high school students. Its director told a local paper in 2021 that Christian, Muslim and Jewish children attend. Registration is open for 2026–27.

entries.name: Nasha Shkola Charter School
entries.purpose: A public charter school for students interested in Russian language and culture. MinnPost reported in 2016 that the Slavic Community Center established it in 2012, and placed the school in Minnetonka at that time. The school says 95 percent of its students speak Russian at home or have a Russian-speaking parent. The name means Our School.

entries.name: American Russian Center
entries.purpose: Formerly Russian Soul, renamed in 2023. A 501(c)(3) for Russian speakers offering events, language classes, immersion camps and a children's theater returning in fall 2026.

entries.name: Theatre Novi Most
entries.purpose: Founded in 1998 by Russian director Vladimir Rovinsky and American director Lisa Channer to develop new international work. Recently raised money for emergency legal fees for Ukrainian refugees in Minneapolis.

entries.name: Lesnoe Ozero
entries.purpose: Russian-language immersion village for young people.

entries.name: East-West Connections
entries.purpose: Promotes understanding between people from the United States, Eastern Europe and Central Asia. Keeps lists of Russian-language churches and language programs in Minnesota.

entries.name: HIAS
entries.purpose: A Jewish refugee protection organization, formerly the Hebrew Immigrant Aid Society. It helped many Soviet Jewish refugees, including the Brin and Spektor families profiled on this page.

entries.name: COJECO
entries.purpose: Formed in 2001; says it represents over 30 network organizations of Russian-speaking Jewish immigrants in New York, with adult, teen and family programs.
aliases: Council of Jewish Émigré Community Organizations

entries.name: Russian Orthodox Church Outside of Russia, Synod of Bishops
entries.purpose: The governing synod of the church. Its U.S. dioceses include the Eastern American Diocese and the Diocese of Chicago and Mid-America.

entries.name: ROCOR Diocese of Chicago and Mid-America
entries.purpose: Led by Bishop Spyridon. Its parish list places Minnesota in its Second Deanery, with St. Panteleimon in Minneapolis.

entries.name: Congress of Russian Americans
entries.purpose: Founded in 1973. Describes itself as a voice of Russian Americans, with humanitarian programs for children and families in crisis.

entries.name: Zerkalo
entries.purpose: Russian-language magazine of the Twin Cities, begun by Leonid Grichener as a newsletter in 1990. The company also publishes a Russian Yellow Pages of Minnesota. Latest issue posted: August–September 2026.

entries.name: North Star
entries.purpose: Russian-language national, international and community news. Issues posted through October 2026.

entries.name: Twin Cities Guide for Russian Speakers
entries.purpose: A guide to places relevant to Russian speakers in Minneapolis and St. Paul, written for recent arrivals and anyone learning about the community. Updated in October 2026.

entries.name: Kontinent
entries.purpose: Russian-language news, analysis and podcasts. Describes itself as a leading conservative site of Russian-speaking America.

entries.name: Meduza
entries.purpose: Independent news about Russia in Russian and English.

entries.name: Dozhd
entries.purpose: Independent Russian-language news channel, also called TV Rain.

entries.name: Current Time
entries.purpose: Russian-language news with sections for Russia, Ukraine, Belarus, Moldova, the Baltics, the Caucasus and Central Asia.

entries.name: Novaya Gazeta Europe
entries.purpose: News on Russia, Belarus and Ukraine in Russian and English. Its editor-in-chief is Kirill Martynov.

entries.name: Radio Svoboda
entries.purpose: The Russian-language service of Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty, with news and investigations.
